basis.text: The record is divided on whether he died before or after midnight. Butterfield (sworn testimony of 29 Mar 1864, p. 434) says it was reported on the night of the 2d that he lay wounded and that he was dead when found; Doubleday (report of 14 Dec 1863, p. 260) names the third day, and the Vermont and Pennsylvania volumes have him found alive; Meade's dispatch of 3 July 8 a.m. (27/1 p. 74) and a Times special of 7:45 a.m. have the body within the lines; Longstreet (27/2 p. 362) dates the wound to the evening of 2 July.

default.label: Wounded the evening of Jul 2; died between that night and about 08:00 on Jul 3; day and hour not settled
default.basis_text: Lower bound: the wound on the evening of Jul 2 (Longstreet's report of 27 Jul 1863, Hall's report of 17 Jul). Upper bound: Meade's dispatch of Jul 3, 8 a.m., and a Times special of 7:45 a.m., which already have the body within the lines. Inside the window the record is divided: Butterfield (sworn, 1864) has him dead when found on the night of the 2d; Doubleday (report of Dec 1863), the Vermont volume and the 149th Pennsylvania have him found alive, dying later and Doubleday naming the third day. No one gives an hour.
default.note: Two parts kept apart: the wound (Jul 2 evening, position P4, documented) and the death (window, P5). 'Jul 2' (P1) and 'Jul 3' (P2) each stay selectable with the witnesses that say them.

animation.note: No hour is documented for the death; nothing is drawn at an instant inside the window. The window shows the span from the evening of Jul 2 to about 08:00 on Jul 3 and the body is within the lines from the upper bound.

witness.name: Daniel Butterfield
witness.role: Major General, chief of staff of the Army of the Potomac

support.note: Butterfield says that 'before the battle was over (on the night of the 2d) it was reported that General Barksdale was on the field wounded, and desired to be brought in; but he died before we reached him. I sent for him, but he was dead when found.' He is the only witness found who dates the death to the night of the 2d; he does not give an hour or say whether midnight had passed, and the sentence is a recollection 270 days later. reason_not_chosen.text: Butterfield, who sent for him, says he was dead when found on the night of the 2d; Doubleday, Vermont and the 149th Pennsylvania have him alive when brought in. The record is divided, so both stay.

inference.step: Butterfield, who sent for Barksdale, says it was reported 'on the night of the 2d' that he lay wounded and wanted to be brought in, and that 'he died before we reached him ... he was dead when found'. Read together, the death comes during the night of the 2d, which is Jul 2 only if the night is taken as before midnight; no hour is stated.
from: Butterfield testimony of 29 Mar 1864 (Joint Committee, p. 434)

inference.step: Wounded in the evening of Jul 2 (Longstreet). Butterfield (1864) puts the death on the night of the 2d, dead when found; Doubleday, the Vermont volume (word came 'during the night') and the 149th Pennsylvania have him found alive and dying later; 'died that night' (New York, 1900); dead within the lines at 8 a. m. and 7:45 a. m. of Jul 3 (Meade, Times). Joined, the death falls between the evening of Jul 2 and about 08:00 on Jul 3. No source gives an hour or says whether midnight had passed.

weighing.summary: Two questions, kept apart. The wound: Longstreet (27 Jul 1863) dates it to the evening of Jul 2; Hall, Jacobs and McLaws place it in the fighting of that day; nobody disputes it. The death: no witness gives an hour. Dead by about 08:00 of Jul 3 is fixed by Meade's dispatch (rank 6) and a Times special (rank 4). Inside that bound the record is divided. Butterfield, Meade's chief of staff, swore in March 1864 that on the night of the 2d it was reported Barksdale lay wounded, 'he died before we reached him. I sent for him, but he was dead when found'; he sent for him himself, which counts for him, but the passage is a recollection after 270 days, an early narrative, and gives no hour. Doubleday's report of Dec 1863 (rank 3, 164 days after) names 'the third day' and says his staff officer brought him in; Doubleday relays rather than saw, and the Vermont volume, the 149th Pennsylvania ('the next day he died') and Doubleday in 1882 ('soon after') have him alive when brought in, all later books or relayed. Butterfield outranks none of them on the rubric by enough to settle it, and none outranks him: the best-placed witnesses disagree, so the death is a window, not a day. It is inferred, not documented, because no source states the day and hour. Doubleday's day name is a day, not an hour, and 'the night of the 2d' is not clearly before midnight. Also read and undated: Hancock (27/1 p. 371, 'left on the field, mortally wounded'), the Duncan medical history ('died in a Union hospital') and a New York address of 1902 ('in the presence of a Union general'). The first delegated 'open gap' is replaced because sources were found, not because an hour was.
weighing.who: Meade commanded the army and wrote from headquarters; Butterfield was his chief of staff and says he sent for Barksdale; Doubleday commanded the division in whose lines Barksdale was brought and his staff officer Livingston brought him in; Longstreet commanded Barksdale's corps and McLaws his division; Hall's brigade stood where he fell; the Times correspondent was with the army. The Pennsylvania regiment history was written by survivors of the unit that found him; the Vermont and New York volumes are by compilers. Nobody who attended the death wrote an account that is local.
weighing.when: Meade's dispatch and the Times special are of the morning of Jul 3 (hours after the event); Hall 15 days; Longstreet 25 days; Doubleday 164 days (report) and 19 years (1882); Butterfield 270 days (testimony of 29 Mar 1864); Jacobs 1864; McLaws 1878; the regiment and state volumes 1900-1916. The earliest two say only that he was dead.
weighing.where: Doubleday's report relays what his staff officer did; the Times correspondent and Meade relay what prisoners and staff told them ('Prisoners report ...'); Longstreet commanded the corps and writes of the attack in general; Hall's brigade stood where he fell, within 20 yards of the Seventh Michigan. The place of death is a hospital within the Union lines; the Historic American Buildings Survey record of the Hummelbaugh house (Park Service programme) says he died at the house and was buried there but gives no date.
weighing.how_knew: Butterfield says he sent for him and found him dead, so his knowledge is of his own orders, though he gives the night of the 2d for the report and no hour for the death. Doubleday, Meade and the Times relay: none says he saw the death. Hall saw the repulse and the fall. The 1914 and 1900 volumes retell unit stories. So the date of death rests on conflicting accounts, which is why the tier is inferred and the class irreducible.
weighing.clock: Clock readings: Meade's 8 a.m. is the Union headquarters clock and the Times 7:45 a newspaper's; the Union and Confederate clocks reportedly differed by about 20 minutes and no row corrects for it. The upper bound (about 08:00 on Jul 3) is read to within that uncertainty; the bound is not used to date the death within the night.
weighing.independence: Groups: Meade's dispatch (one group); the Times correspondent (a separate telegram, though he may draw on the same headquarters talk); Butterfield (sworn testimony; he served at Meade's headquarters, but the passage is his own account of his own errand); Doubleday (report and book of 1882, one author; the Minnesota history quotes him for the last messages and writes 'dying on the third' in its own words, and is counted with his group only as an assumption); the 149th Pennsylvania; the Vermont volume; the New York volume. The window rests on Longstreet (wound), Meade and the Times (upper bound); the day inside it is carried by Butterfield on one side and Doubleday, Vermont and Pennsylvania on the other. The wound rests on Longstreet, Hall, McLaws and Jacobs, four independent groups.

source_panel_text: Wounded the evening of Jul 2 (Longstreet). Death: the record is divided. Butterfield swore he was dead when found on the night of the 2d; Doubleday names the third day and others have him found alive. Meade's 8 a.m. dispatch has the body within the lines. The window runs to about 08:00 on Jul 3; no hour; two other values listed.

what_would_change_it: An account by Lt. Col. C. E. Livingston, a Union or Confederate surgeon at the Hummelbaugh house, or a member of Barksdale's staff or of the detail of the 13th Vermont that carried him in, giving the hour of death; a Mississippi regimental history or letter of 1863 dating it; the page image of Butterfield's testimony (the digits were not seen on the page); the page of the plan's Stone Sentinels source. A time before midnight would move the window to the night of Jul 2; a time after would settle Jul 3.
